weeks.title: The Meaning of Baptism
weeks.theme: Baptism obeys Jesus’ command and publicly testifies that I died, was buried and rose with Christ.
group: What impressions or hesitations did you have about baptism?
How do you understand “dying, being buried and rising with Christ”?
Is anything holding you back from baptism?
weeks.guide: This week begins baptism preparation. Help them understand: baptism isn’t a condition of salvation (the thief on the cross was saved without it), but it is a believer’s first step of obedience and a public testimony. Learn their hesitations—fear of family opposition, fear of failing, feeling not good enough—and walk through each one. Explain your church’s baptism process (class, interview, date, mode). Open the “Baptism Preparation” checklist on the Journey tab together.
weeks.meet: This week, look at “Baptism Preparation” on the Journey tab with the person walking with you, and talk honestly about your thoughts and hesitations.
weeks.keyText: We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.

lessons.title: Jesus’ Command
text: Jesus came to them and spoke to them, saying, “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth.
Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,
teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age.” Amen.
lessons.hear:
After rising and before ascending, Jesus gave his disciples his final instructions: “All authority has been given to me in heaven and on earth. Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all things that I commanded you. Behold, I am with you always, even to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:18-20).

This is called the Great Commission. Jesus places baptism within the process of making disciples: someone shares the gospel, people believe, then they are baptized and learn to obey Jesus’ teaching. Baptism isn’t an optional religious ritual; it is Jesus’ own command. In the early church, believers were baptized as soon as they believed, often the same day.

Why be baptized? The simplest reason: because Jesus said so. When you love someone, you are willing to do what they ask. Baptism is a believer’s first public act of obedience, like a wedding where people who love each other make a public promise. And Jesus’ final promise: “I am with you always.” You don’t take this step alone; he is with you.
lessons.light: Letting Jesus reign means doing what he says. Baptism is the first step of obedience: not because I feel I need it, but because the Lord commands it. An obedient heart is a selfless heart.
think: Where does Jesus place baptism in making disciples?
How do you think baptism relates to salvation?
Is “because Jesus said so” a convincing reason for you?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you command those who believe in you to be baptized. I want to obey your word—not in order to be saved, but because you have saved me and I love you. Prepare my heart and lead me on the road to baptism. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Ask the person walking with you or your church: what is the baptism process? When is the next baptism? Note it on the Journey tab.
lessons.quick: Baptism isn’t to be saved; it’s obedience because we are saved.

lessons.title: Died, Buried, Raised
text: Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.
lessons.hear:
The word “baptize” originally means “to immerse.” In the early church, people were immersed in water and then came up out of it. The picture is full of meaning. Paul says: “Or don’t you know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:3-4).

Going under the water pictures the old self dying and being buried with Christ; coming up out of the water pictures the new self rising with Christ. It’s like a funeral and a birthday party at once: burying the old self who lived centered on self, insisting on being in charge, and welcoming a new self centered on Jesus, letting Jesus be Lord.

The water itself has no magic power and can’t wash away sin; what truly cleanses us is Jesus’ blood. But baptism is a visible sign declaring something invisible yet real: I have been united with Christ. Later, when you feel weak, you can remember your baptism day and tell yourself: “That old me has been buried. I am a new creation.”
lessons.light: Baptism is the public sign of the old self-centered life becoming the new selfless life. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” becomes a lifelong practice beginning that day.
think: What do you think of the “funeral plus birthday party” picture?
What do you most want to “bury” at your baptism?
After baptism, how could remembering this day help you when you are weak?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, in baptism I want to declare that my old, self-centered life has died and been buried with you, and my new, Christ-centered life has risen with you. Let me walk in newness of life in all I do. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write “The old self I will bury” (three habits or attitudes) and “The new self I will welcome” (three new ways). You can bring it on your baptism day.
lessons.quick: Baptism: the old self buried, the new self raised.

lessons.title: A Public Testimony
text: Peter said to them, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.
Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls.
lessons.hear:
On the day of Pentecost, Peter preached to the crowds in Jerusalem. Many were cut to the heart and asked, “What shall we do?” Peter said: “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38). And “Then those who gladly received his word were baptized. There were added that day about three thousand souls” (Acts 2:41).

In Jerusalem at that time, being publicly baptized into Jesus’ name was very bold, because the city had just crucified him. Baptism publicly announced: “I belong to Jesus.” That is why baptism usually happens before others, not in private: faith is personal, but not private.

In Chinese communities today, baptism is often the step that takes the most courage: family may not understand, friends may not get it. But public testimony has power. It helps you settle your decision, lets those around you know about your change, and surrounds you with brothers and sisters who witness and cheer. You don’t believe in secret; you follow the Lord openly.
lessons.light: Following the Lord publicly takes courage and humility: no longer caring about people’s opinions, but about Jesus’ heart. The focus is Jesus—not others, and not our circumstances.
think: Whose reaction to a public baptism worries you most?
“Faith is personal, but not private”—what do you think?
Who would you like to witness your baptism?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I want to acknowledge publicly that I belong to you. I am worried about ___’s reaction; give me courage, and wisdom and love to face it. Let my baptism be a testimony to your glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: List the people you’d like to invite to your baptism (family, friends, coworkers) and pray for each one.
lessons.quick: Faith is personal, but not private.

lessons.title: What Is Keeping Me?
text: Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus.
As they went on the way, they came to some water; and the eunuch said, “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?”
He commanded the chariot to stand still, and they both went down into the water, both Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him.
lessons.hear:
An Ethiopian official was riding in his chariot reading Isaiah, but he didn’t understand it. God sent Philip to the chariot. Philip asked, “Do you understand what you are reading?” The official said, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” So “Philip opened his mouth, and beginning from this Scripture, preached to him about Jesus” (Acts 8:35).

As they traveled they came to some water, and the official said, “Behold, here is water. What is keeping me from being baptized?” (Acts 8:36). Philip baptized him. He hadn’t taken years of classes or waited until he was “good enough”; as soon as he understood the gospel and truly believed, he longed to be baptized.

Many want to be baptized yet have many “hindrances” in their hearts: “I’m not good enough,” “I’m afraid I’ll sin again after baptism,” “my family will object,” “I don’t know the Bible well.” These deserve honest attention, but we should also ask: are they really hindrances? Baptism isn’t a graduation ceremony but an enrollment ceremony; it doesn’t prove you are already very spiritual, but declares that you are starting to follow the Lord. You don’t need to be perfect to be baptized; you only need to truly believe in Jesus and be willing to follow him.
lessons.light: “I’m not good enough” sounds humble, but it is often another form of self-reliance: I must achieve something before I deserve baptism. Baptism is a sign of grace, not a certificate of merit. Lay down your own standard and receive God’s grace.
think: What reasons in your heart “hinder” you from baptism?
How does “baptism is an enrollment, not a graduation” help you?
Do you, like the official, long to be baptized?
lessons.speak: Lord, there are things in my heart that make me hesitate: ___. Help me discern which need to be addressed and which are only my fears. I want to long to obey you like that official. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write down each of your “hindrances” and discuss them with the person walking with you: which can be dealt with before baptism, and which you can carry forward together?
lessons.quick: Baptism is an enrollment ceremony, not a graduation.

lessons.title: After Baptism
text: They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer.
Fear came on every soul, and many wonders and signs were done through the apostles.
All who believed were together, and had all things in common.
They sold their possessions and goods, and distributed them to all, according as anyone had need.
lessons.hear:
After those three thousand were baptized, they didn’t just go home and that was that. The Bible describes their life: “They continued steadfastly in the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and prayer” (Acts 2:42). Baptism is a beginning; then comes a new way of life: learning God’s word (the apostles’ teaching), living in community (fellowship), remembering the Lord (breaking bread), and prayer.

They even “had all things in common,” sharing with anyone in need and caring for one another. It was a spiritual family full of love. When someone is baptized, they are placed into a family: with spiritual parents, brothers and sisters, growing, serving and experiencing God together.

So the most important thing after baptism is not to walk the road of faith alone. Keep reading the Bible and praying, attend gatherings, join a home group, find a spiritual parent to walk with you, and find spiritual companions to grow with. This week we saw the meaning of baptism. Next week we look more deeply at the change of life baptism represents—from old self to new, from self-centered to selfless.
lessons.light: Baptism isn’t a personal finish line but the start of life in God’s family. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: new life grows in relationships and is fed in a spiritual home.
think: Of the early church’s four habits, which do you most need to begin?
What does a “spiritual family” look like in your mind?
After baptism, who do you hope will keep walking with you?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that you didn’t only save me but placed me in your family. After baptism, help me continue steadfastly in your word, in fellowship with brothers and sisters, in remembering the Lord, and in prayer. Let me not walk this road alone. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Ask the person walking with you: which home group can I join after baptism? Which gatherings can I attend? Record it on the Journey tab.
lessons.quick: Baptism is the beginning of life in God’s family, not the end.

weeks.title: A Changed Life: Old Self and New Self
weeks.theme: From the old self-centered life to the new selfless life: it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
group: Where do you see signs of a “self-centered” life in yourself?
How do you understand “no longer I, but Christ”?
What could humility look like in your daily life?
weeks.guide: This week introduces the core of 321: self-centered versus selfless. New believers may hear “selfless” and think it means “having no self, losing yourself.” Explain: selfless doesn’t mean nothing; it means no longer centering life on myself, letting Jesus live in me; it isn’t losing yourself but entering the infinite and living out your true self. Use concrete examples: self-centered (fighting over who’s right, saving face, needing control, self-pity) versus selfless (listening first, apologizing first, helping others succeed). This is also a great week to share your own testimony of change.
weeks.meet: This week, each share one “self-centered” experience and one “selfless” experience with the person walking with you. How were the outcomes different?
weeks.keyText: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

lessons.title: Put Off the Old, Put On the New
text: that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit,
and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind,
and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.
lessons.hear:
At baptism, some churches dress the candidates in white robes. The picture comes from Paul’s teaching: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth” (Ephesians 4:22-24).

The old self is like a worn-out, smelly garment that keeps getting worse; the new self is a new garment God has made for you in his likeness. Putting off and putting on is a choice we make every day. Each morning you choose what to wear; likewise, each day you choose: will I live as the old self or the new self today?

Notice the phrase in the middle: “be renewed in the spirit of your mind.” The key to changing clothes is the mind—our beliefs and ways of thinking. Change the mindset and you change the life: when you believe “I am a new self,” you will live more and more like one. It’s like a prince who wandered the streets for years; back in the palace, he has to learn to stop thinking like a beggar and start thinking like a prince.
lessons.light: Changing the mindset changes the life; changing the life changes how we live. Putting off the old and putting on the new starts with a renewed mind. This is change from the inside out: mindset, life, living, relationships, ministry.
think: Which “old clothes” of the old self do you still often wear?
What belief in you needs to be “renewed in the spirit of your mind”?
What does the prince-in-the-palace picture bring to mind?
lessons.speak: Lord, today I want to put off the old self and put on the new self you have prepared for me. Renew my mind, so I see myself, others and everything with the eyes of the new self. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: As you dress in the morning, say in your heart: “Today I put off the old self and put on the new.” Choose one old habit to “put off,” and deliberately skip it today.
lessons.quick: Every morning, choose to put on the new self.

lessons.title: Self-Centered: Me at the Center
text: He said to all, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.
For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake will save it.
lessons.hear:
321 uses a simple word for the root human problem: being “self-centered.” It means making myself the center, insisting on being master and king. It shows itself in many ways: saving face, needing to win, needing control, needing to be seen, being unable to take criticism, thinking of myself first. The self-centered life is the root of humanity’s fall, and it shows itself as pride.

Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). “Deny himself” means to stop making self the center. Then Jesus said something that sounds contradictory: “For whoever desires to save his life will lose it, but whoever will lose his life for my sake will save it” (Luke 9:24). The tighter you grip, the more you lose; let go, and you gain.

It’s like a clenched fist that can’t hold anything; only an open hand can receive a gift. The self-centered grip “my rights, my face, my way,” and the result is broken relationships and inner unrest; those who deny themselves let go and gain peace, relationships and real life. Self-denial isn’t done once; it is a “daily” choice.
lessons.light: The self-centered life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of our problems. Self-denial is living for Jesus and for others, not for self—taking up our cross and following the Lord. Seeing our self-centeredness is where change begins.
think: Of the signs of self-centeredness (saving face, winning, control…), which shows up most in you?
“The tighter you grip, the more you lose”—have you experienced that?
Where could you “deny yourself” today?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I see so much self-centeredness in me: I want face, I want to win, I want control. Forgive me. I am willing to deny myself daily, take up my cross and follow you, unclench my fist and receive your life. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Today, in an argument or a frustrating moment, deliberately “don’t win” once: listen to the other person fully and step back first. Notice what happens.
lessons.quick: A clenched fist can’t receive a gift; an open hand receives life.

lessons.title: No Longer I
text: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.
lessons.hear:
Paul wrote the most central sentence of the Christian life: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

What does “no longer I” mean? Not that Paul disappeared or lost his personality, but that the master of his life changed. Before, “I” was in the driver’s seat; now Christ is. This is what 321 calls “selfless”: selfless doesn’t mean nothing; it means entering the infinite and living out the infinite. When my limited self steps aside, the infinite Christ lives out his life in me.

Picture a glove: by itself it can do nothing, but when a hand slips inside, the glove can write, play music and embrace someone. We are like the glove; Christ is the hand. We don’t have to make ourselves saints by effort; we let Christ live in us. And the motive is warm: “who loved me and gave himself up for me.” We deny ourselves because he first gave himself for us.
lessons.light: Selfless: no longer I, but Christ; not I who live, but Christ who lives in me. Only the selfless can be one with Christ; only the selfless can let Jesus reign. This is the heart of the new life.
think: Who is in the “driver’s seat” of your life right now?
What does the glove picture help you understand?
How does “who loved me and gave himself up for me” become your motive for self-denial?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I am willing to be crucified with you. From now on, it is no longer I who live, but you who live in me. I give you the driver’s seat; live your life in me. Because you loved me and gave yourself for me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Memorize Galatians 2:20. At least three times today, tell yourself: “No longer I, but Christ.”
lessons.quick: It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.

lessons.title: Humility Is the Key
text: But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.”
Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you.
lessons.hear:
James says: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4:6). This is a spiritual law as real as gravity. Water flows downhill, and so does God’s grace. The prouder we are, the less grace we receive; the humbler we are, the more we experience God’s grace.

321 defines pride and humility clearly: pride is leaving our place and grabbing authority—leaving our place as humans, grabbing God’s authority, wanting to replace God. Humility is laying down authority and returning to our place—returning to our human place, letting go of God’s authority, letting people be people and God be God. So humility isn’t inferiority or thinking poorly of yourself; humility is acknowledging that God is God and I am human.

The same law works in relationships: pride provokes pride; pride against pride, both sides lose. Humility brings out humility; humility meeting humility, both win. James continues: “Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he will exalt you” (James 4:10). Humility is the key to revival—and the key to a changed life.
lessons.light: Humility is the key to revival; God gives grace to the humble and opposes the proud. Pride leaves its place and grabs authority; humility lays down authority and returns to its place. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan.
think: “Water flows downhill, and so does grace”—have you experienced it?
What is the difference between humility and inferiority?
In which relationship do you most need “humility bringing out humility”?
lessons.speak: God, I often leave my place and grab authority that isn’t mine, wanting to be in charge in your place. Forgive my pride. I humble myself before you, return to my place as a human, and let you be God. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Today, say to someone, “That was my fault,” or “Thank you—I need you,” letting humility bring out humility.
lessons.quick: Let people be people and God be God—that is humility.

lessons.title: Change the Mindset, Change the Life
text: Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.
lessons.hear:
Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). “Transformed” is the word used for a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. Real change begins with a renewed mind.

321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change how you live. How does a mindset change? From a human perspective to God’s perspective, from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one, from a temporary perspective to an eternal one, from a worldly perspective to a godly one. Change the perspective and you change the mindset.

There are eight steps to changing a mindset: Information (hearing truth), Revelation (the Spirit’s light), Conviction (accepting it in the heart), Practice (doing it), Review (looking back), Adjustment (correcting), Repetition (practicing again and again), and Multiplication (teaching others). This week we saw the change of life baptism represents. Next week we will turn your change into a testimony, because your story may be where someone else begins to know God.
lessons.light: The eight steps of changing a mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Practice, Review, Adjustment, Repetition, Multiplication. Moving from a human perspective to God’s, life begins to be transformed. Change starts with me.
think: Over these months, which belief of yours has God changed most?
Of the eight steps, where are you now?
In what area do you most want to stop “being conformed to this world”?
lessons.speak: God, renew my mind so that I’m no longer conformed to this world but see everything from your perspective. I’m willing to let you change my mindset, and so change my life and how I live. Change starts with me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write: “I used to think…, now I understand…”—at least three times. This will be material for your testimony.
lessons.quick: Change the mindset, change the life; change the life, change how you live.

weeks.title: My Testimony
weeks.theme: Your life story testifies to God’s grace; be ready to share the reason for your hope with gentleness.
group: In your journey to faith (or seeking), what was the key moment?
What has changed in your life before and after?
Who do you most want to tell your story to?
weeks.guide: This week, help them write their testimony (the Journey tab has a testimony writer). A good testimony has three parts: me before faith, how I came to know Jesus, how my life has changed. Three to five minutes, concrete and true, centered on Jesus, not exaggerated, not criticizing others. Ask them to tell it to you aloud first, then help them shape it. Baptism services often include a testimony, so this week is ideal preparation. Remind them: a testimony isn’t performing success, but honestly telling of God’s grace.
weeks.meet: This week, ask the person walking with you to listen to your story (five minutes) and give you one encouragement and one suggestion.
weeks.keyText: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,

lessons.title: Go Home and Tell Your Family
text: As he was entering into the boat, he who had been possessed by demons begged him that he might be with him.
He didn’t allow him, but said to him, “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you.”
He went his way, and began to proclaim in Decapolis how Jesus had done great things for him, and everyone marveled.
lessons.hear:
A man possessed by many demons lived among the tombs, crying out day and night and cutting himself with stones; no one could bind him. Jesus drove out the demons, and the man was clothed, in his right mind, sitting at Jesus’ feet. He begged to go with Jesus, but Jesus said to him: “Go to your house, to your friends, and tell them what great things the Lord has done for you and how he had mercy on you” (Mark 5:19).

This man had no theological training. He had only one thing to say: what Jesus had done for him. The result? “He went his way, and began to proclaim in Decapolis how Jesus had done great things for him, and everyone marveled” (Mark 5:20). His testimony affected a whole region.

You don’t need to be a theologian to share your faith; you only need to tell what God has done for you. No one can argue with your story, because you lived it. Maybe your story isn’t dramatic—that’s fine; God’s grace in an ordinary life is just as precious. Today, start thinking: what has the Lord done for me?
lessons.light: The focus of a testimony isn’t “how good I am” but “what great things the Lord has done for me.” Let Jesus receive all the glory: the main character of a testimony is Jesus, not me.
think: If you summed up in one sentence what the Lord has done for you, what would you say?
Why did Jesus send this man home to tell his story instead of letting him come along?
Among your family and friends, who most needs to hear your story?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for doing great things for me and having mercy on me. I want to tell my family what you have done for me. Give me courage, and the right time and words. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write one sentence: “The great thing the Lord has done for me is…”
lessons.quick: I may not know theology, but I know what the Lord has done for me.

lessons.title: Once I Was Blind
text: So they called the man who was blind a second time, and said to him, “Give glory to God. We know that this man is a sinner.”
He therefore answered, “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see.”
lessons.hear:
Jesus healed a man born blind. The religious leaders were unhappy because Jesus healed on the Sabbath. Wanting to prove Jesus was a sinner, they summoned the man and said, “We know that this man is a sinner.” The man gave a powerful answer: “I don’t know if he is a sinner. One thing I do know: that though I was blind, now I see” (John 9:25).

He didn’t debate theology with scholars or answer every question. He simply said the one thing he knew: once I was blind, now I see. That is where a testimony’s power lies: it isn’t theory but experience; not argument but fact.

Your testimony can be this simple: I used to…, now I…. I used to be anxious; now I have peace. I used to lose my temper; now I’m learning to listen first. I used to feel life was meaningless; now I know who I live for. You don’t have to answer every question about faith; you only need to tell honestly the change you know.
lessons.light: A testimony’s power is its truth. Don’t exaggerate or polish; just honestly tell “then” and “now.” Honesty is humility, and a humble testimony moves people most.
think: If you used “I used to…, now I…,” what would you say?
The man didn’t answer every question, only what he knew. How does that encourage you?
What is the clearest “then” and “now” in your life?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I used to be ___, now I ___. Thank you for opening my eyes. I don’t need to know every answer; I only need to tell honestly what you have done in me. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write three pairs of “I used to…, now I….”
lessons.quick: One thing I know: once I was blind, now I see.

lessons.title: The Three Parts of a Testimony
text: The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief.
However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life.
lessons.hear:
Paul wrote to his spiritual son Timothy and told his own testimony in a few lines: “The saying is faithful and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief. However, for this cause I obtained mercy, that in me first, Jesus Christ might display all his patience for an example of those who were going to believe in him for eternal life” (1 Timothy 1:15-16).

Paul’s testimony has three clear parts: once I was the chief of sinners (before faith); I obtained mercy (how I came to know Jesus); to be an example to those who would believe later (the change and calling after faith). This is the best structure for writing a testimony. Part one, me before faith: how did I live? What was missing in my heart? Part two, how I came to know Jesus: what person, event or verse turned me toward God? Part three, life after faith: what is different now?

A few principles: be concrete (real events and feelings, not just “I felt empty”), be true (no exaggeration or polish), be Jesus-centered (focus on him, not yourself), be brief (three to five minutes), and avoid criticizing others or using church jargon. “My Testimony” on the Journey tab can help you write it one part at a time.
lessons.light: Paul calls himself the “chief of sinners”—that’s humility; he “obtained mercy”—that’s grace; he would be an “example”—that’s calling. A testimony is: seeing my own problem, seeing God’s grace, living a new life.
think: Of the three parts, which is easiest for you to write? Which is hardest?
Your part two—what person or event turned you toward God?
What kind of person do you hope your testimony will help?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for coming into the world to save sinners like me. I have obtained mercy. Help me write my testimony, so it becomes an example for those who will come to know you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Open “My Testimony” on the Journey tab and write three to five sentences for each part. You can ask Xiaozhi to help polish it, but keep your own voice.
lessons.quick: Me before, meeting Jesus, me now—that’s a testimony.

lessons.title: Always Be Ready
text: But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear,
lessons.hear:
Peter says: “But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts. Always be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you a reason concerning the hope that is in you, with humility and fear” (1 Peter 3:15). “Always be ready” is like carrying an umbrella: you don’t know when it will rain, but if you’re prepared you won’t panic.

A friend might ask, “Why did you start believing in Jesus?” A coworker might say, “You seem different lately.” A family member might challenge, “What good does that faith do?” These are all chances to share. Someone prepared can naturally tell a two- or three-minute story; someone unprepared might only say, “Um… it just seemed good.”

Preparation includes three things: your story (testimony); one or two core lines of the gospel (for example, Romans 6:23 or John 3:16); and your attitude—gentle and respectful. Not debating or selling, but sharing good news the way you’d recommend a great restaurant: sincerely and naturally. Leave the results to God; you just tell it honestly.
lessons.light: Sanctifying the Lord in our hearts means letting Jesus reign there. Prepared but not pushy, gentle yet confident—this is selfless sharing: the focus is the other person’s need, not how well I speak.
think: If someone asked you tomorrow, “Why do you believe in Jesus?” what would you say?
How important are gentleness and respect when sharing faith?
In what settings are you most likely to be asked about your faith?
lessons.speak: Lord, I want to always be ready, so that when someone asks the reason for my hope, I can answer with gentleness and respect. Give me opportunities, and wisdom and love. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Record yourself telling a three-minute testimony on your phone. Listen once and notice where it could be clearer and more natural.
lessons.quick: Carry your story the way you carry an umbrella.

lessons.title: The Word of Their Testimony
text: They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death.
lessons.hear:
Revelation describes how believers overcome Satan, the accuser: “They overcame him because of the Lamb’s blood, and because of the word of their testimony. They didn’t love their life, even to death” (Revelation 12:11). Two keys to victory: the Lamb’s blood—Jesus’ work on the cross; and the word of their testimony—believers telling what God has done in them.

This tells us that testimony isn’t only sharing; it is spiritual warfare. Every time you say, “God saved me; God changed me,” you declare that Satan’s lies (“you don’t deserve it,” “there’s no hope,” “you can’t change”) are broken. Telling your testimony to yourself strengthens your faith; telling it to others gives them hope.

This week you wrote your testimony. Perhaps at your baptism you will tell it before everyone; perhaps over a family dinner you will quietly tell your relatives. Wherever it is, your story is a record of God’s grace. Next week we prepare for baptism day and learn the meaning of the Lord’s Supper.
lessons.light: Selflessness overcomes Satan; victory comes by the Lamb’s blood and the word of testimony. A testimony isn’t boasting about myself but proclaiming Jesus’ victory; giving all the glory to Jesus is the most powerful testimony.
think: Why do you think telling your testimony is also spiritual warfare?
What lies does Satan often use against you? How does your testimony answer them?
Are you ready to share your testimony at baptism?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you that your blood has won the victory for me, and thank you for your work in me. I want to tell my testimony and proclaim your victory. Let Satan’s lies lose their power over me, and let you receive all the glory. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Tell your testimony to a Christian friend, and save the finished testimony on the Journey tab.
lessons.quick: They overcame by the Lamb’s blood and the word of their testimony.

weeks.title: Baptism and the Lord’s Supper
weeks.theme: Baptism is a once-for-all public declaration; the Lord’s Supper is a lifelong remembrance. Both join us to Christ and his body.
group: Before baptism, what do you want to entrust to God or examine?
What does the Lord’s Supper mean to you?
After baptism, how do you most want to follow the Lord?
weeks.guide: This is baptism week (or the final preparation before baptism). Help them do a pre-baptism self-examination (not self-condemnation but entrusting), and confirm the date, process, what to bring and which friends and family to invite. On the day, be sure to be there, take photos, and give them a blessing (you can make a baptism blessing card in the card studio). Afterward, remind them to record their baptism date on the Journey tab, and contact them often over the next two weeks to help them settle into a home group.
weeks.meet: This week, pray a pre-baptism prayer of self-examination with the person walking with you, and make final preparations for baptism day.
weeks.keyText: For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.

lessons.title: Self-Examination Before Baptism
text: Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts.
See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way.
lessons.hear:
David prayed a very brave prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23-24). This isn’t a fearful prayer but a trusting one: David believed God searched him not to condemn him but to lead him.

The days before baptism are a good time for this kind of examination. Not tearing yourself apart, but like sorting luggage before moving into a new home: what comes with you and what gets thrown out. Ask yourself before God: is there sin I haven’t yet handed to him? Someone I haven’t forgiven? An idol (anything that takes God’s place) I haven’t let go of? Something I need to return or apologize for?

Whatever comes to mind, confess it honestly to God and receive his forgiveness. What you can deal with, deal with (apologize, return, remove idols from your home); what you can’t yet, hand to God, tell the person walking with you, and ask them to pray. Then welcome your baptism day with a light, clean, grateful heart.
lessons.light: Letting God search us is humility. Self-examination isn’t self-condemnation but entrusting: handing God what we haven’t yet given him. We see our own problem, and we see God’s grace.
think: Is there sin or a burden in your heart you haven’t yet given to God?
Is there someone you need to forgive or reconcile with before baptism?
Is there an “idol” in your home or heart you need to let go of?
lessons.speak: God, search me and know my heart; see if there is any wicked way in me. I give you ___; forgive me, cleanse me, and lead me in the everlasting way. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Spend fifteen quiet minutes praying through Psalm 139:23-24. Write down what comes to mind, and this week deal with what you can.
lessons.quick: Before baptism, let God search me and set me in order.

lessons.title: Jesus Was Baptized Too
text: Then Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to John, to be baptized by him.
But John would have hindered him, saying, “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?”
But Jesus, answering, said to him, “Allow it now, for this is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness.” Then he allowed him.
Jesus, when he was baptized, went up directly from the water: and behold, the heavens were opened to him. He saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming on him.
Behold, a voice out of the heavens said, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.”
lessons.hear:
Before beginning his ministry, Jesus went to the Jordan River to be baptized by John. John was astonished: “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” Jesus had no sin and didn’t need to repent—so why be baptized? Jesus said: “Allow it now, for this is the fitting way for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15). Jesus was baptized to stand with us and to set us an example.

Then something wonderful happened: “Jesus, when he was baptized, went up directly from the water: and behold, the heavens were opened to him. He saw the Spirit of God descending as a dove, and coming on him. Behold, a voice out of the heavens said, ‘This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased’” (Matthew 3:16-17). At Jesus’ baptism, Father, Son and Holy Spirit were revealed together.

“This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Notice that Jesus hadn’t yet begun preaching or performed any miracle. The Father was pleased with him not because of his performance but because of who he was. When you are baptized, the Father sees you the same way: in Christ you are his beloved son or daughter, the one he delights in—not because of what you have done, but because you belong to Christ.
lessons.light: Jesus is my example: even the sinless Jesus was humbly baptized to fulfill all righteousness. The Father’s delight rests on identity, not performance. In Christ, I too am a child God delights in.
think: Jesus had no sin—why was he baptized? What does that teach you?
“This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased”—can you believe God says this to you too?
What moment of your baptism day are you most looking forward to?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for saying at Jesus’ baptism, “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased.” Thank you for seeing me this way in Christ too. At my baptism, let me hear you say to me, “You are the one I delight in.” In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Make a verse card with “This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 3:17) as a baptism gift to yourself.
lessons.quick: The Father delights in me not for my performance, but because I belong to Christ.

lessons.title: The Lord’s Supper
text: For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread.
When he had given thanks, he broke it and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.”
In the same way he also took the cup after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.”
For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
lessons.hear:
On the night he was betrayed, Jesus ate a last supper with his disciples. He took bread, gave thanks, broke it and said: “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.” In the same way he took the cup after supper, saying: “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me” (1 Corinthians 11:24-25).

This is the Lord’s Supper (also called Communion or the breaking of bread). Baptism happens once, like being born; the Lord’s Supper happens often, like eating meals. Each time we take it, we remember: Jesus’ body was broken for us, his blood shed for us. Paul says: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26).

The Lord’s Supper faces three directions: looking back, remembering Jesus’ love on the cross; looking within, examining ourselves and making peace with God and others; looking forward, hoping for Jesus’ return. After baptism you can share the Lord’s Supper with your brothers and sisters. Each time is a moment to give thanks again and be strengthened again.
lessons.light: The Lord’s Supper reminds us that everything is what God has done and accomplished in Jesus—all grace. Each time we receive it, we refocus on Jesus, give thanks in everything, and give him the glory.
think: How are baptism and the Lord’s Supper different?
Of the three directions (back, within, forward), which means most to you?
Are you looking forward to your first Communion?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you that your body was broken for me and your blood shed for me. I want to remember you often, examine myself, and hope for your return. Let every Communion be a moment of fresh thanks and fresh strength. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: At dinner, take a piece of bread or a bite of rice and quietly think: Jesus’ body was broken for me. Thank him.
lessons.quick: Baptism is a once-for-all declaration; Communion is a lifelong remembrance.

lessons.title: One Body
text: For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all given to drink into one Spirit.
lessons.hear:
Paul says: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Greeks, whether bond or free; and were all given to drink into one Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:13). Baptism isn’t only between an individual and God; it is being placed into Christ’s body—the church.

In the early church, Jews and Gentiles, slaves and masters were completely separate in society, yet in the church they were baptized together, broke bread together and called one another brothers and sisters. It’s the same today: in the church you will meet people of every age, background and personality, and you become one family because of the same Jesus.

On your baptism day you don’t just receive a certificate; you receive a family. This family isn’t perfect, because it is full of forgiven sinners; but it is precious, because Jesus is in its midst. In stage six we will learn how to live in this family, commit to it and grow—and one day become spiritual parents who lead others home.
lessons.light: Only the selfless can be one. In Christ’s body, no one is above anyone else; we are all forgiven sinners. Baptism joins us to Christ the head and to one another: life first, then relationships.
think: Is “baptism is being placed into a body” the same as your previous understanding?
Are people of different backgrounds in church a blessing or a challenge to you?
What do you hope to receive from—and give to—this church family?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for placing me into your body through baptism and giving me a spiritual family. Help me accept people who are different, and grow, give and love one another in this family. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: At church (or home group), get to know one brother or sister you don’t know well yet. Remember their name and pray for them.
lessons.quick: On baptism day I don’t just get a certificate—I get a family.

lessons.title: Following for Life
text: Walking by the sea of Galilee, he saw two brothers: Simon, who is called Peter, and Andrew, his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen.
He said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men.”
They immediately left their nets and followed him.
lessons.hear:
Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw two fishermen—Peter and his brother Andrew—casting a net. Jesus said to them: “Come after me, and I will make you fishers for men” (Matthew 4:19). They immediately left their nets and followed him.

Following Jesus is a lifelong journey. Peter later stumbled, denied the Lord and failed, yet Jesus found him, restored him and used him again and again. Following isn’t done perfectly at once; it is keeping in step a little more each day. “Fishers for men” also tells us that those who follow Jesus will be changed by him into people who go looking for others and lead them. Those who are found go and find others.

Stage five ends here. You have understood the meaning of baptism, experienced a changed life, written your testimony and prepared for baptism. If you have been baptized, congratulations! Record this important day on the Journey tab. If not yet, keep going and prepare in God’s timing. Next we enter the final stage: committing to a church, joining a home group, and beginning the journey of becoming a spiritual parent.
lessons.light: Following Jesus means letting him reign for a lifetime. Those who were accompanied will go and accompany others; those who were found will go and find others. This is the beginning of building God’s order.
think: “Left their nets”—what might you need to let go of to follow Jesus?
Peter stumbled and was restored all his life. What hope does that give you?
“Fishers for men”—who comes to mind as someone you could walk with someday?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I want to follow you all my life. I know I will stumble, but I believe you will find me again and again. Use me too, so that one day I can walk with others and lead them to know you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: If you have been baptized, record the date on the Journey tab and send a thank-you to the person walking with you. If not yet, agree on a preparation timeline with them.
lessons.quick: Those who are found go and find others.
